title: Aadhaar Is Going Global: UIDAI Working to Let NRIs and OCIs Enrol Without India Stay
excerpt: UIDAI chief Saurabh Vijay told Global Fintech Fest 2026 that proof-of-concept work is underway and a legal framework is being built to give overseas Indians access to the digital ID system.
body:
• UIDAI CEO Saurabh Vijay said at Global Fintech Fest 2026 that the authority is building the legal framework to take Aadhaar international, with proof-of-concept work already underway.
  • The plan includes allowing OCI cardholders to enrol without the current 182-day India stay requirement — a long-standing grievance of the 36-million-strong diaspora.
  • Separately, India's IFSCA is piloting Aadhaar face authentication in the UAE to onboard NRIs digitally, with the pilot expected to extend to the US and two more countries.
  • Under today's rules, NRIs with valid Indian passports can enrol but must visit India in person; OCI holders face a 182-day residency condition.

Aadhaar without the home trip

Sixteen years after its launch, Aadhaar is being readied to go global. The Unique Identification Authority of India is working to extend the country's digital identity system to non-resident Indians and overseas citizens of India, with proof-of-concept work already happening and a new legal framework in the works, UIDAI CEO Saurabh Vijay said at the Global Fintech Fest 2026 in Mumbai.

"I think for Aadhaar, the focus now is making Aadhaar international. We really want to work on the interoperability part of it — how to make it more possible. So already some PoCs (proof of concept) are happening."

— Saurabh Vijay, CEO, UIDAI

The most consequential change under discussion concerns OCI cardholders. Today, an OCI holder can enrol for Aadhaar only as a resident foreign national after spending at least 182 days in India in the 12 months before applying, with Indian address proof. Vijay said UIDAI is developing policies to make Aadhaar available to OCIs without that compulsory stay — aiming, in his words, to help them stay better connected to India's digital and financial ecosystem "so that it brings in more investment."

The rules as they stand

The current regime is a frequent source of confusion. An NRI holding a valid Indian passport can apply for Aadhaar and the 182-day condition does not apply — but enrolment still requires an in-person visit to an Aadhaar Enrolment Centre in India. For OCI cardholders, the residency test applies in full. A 2018 UIDAI circular clarified that most NRIs, PIOs and OCIs are not entitled to Aadhaar under the Aadhaar Act, which defines a "resident" as someone who has spent 182 days or more in India in the preceding 12 months. The global push would effectively create a new lane outside that definition.

The timing is not accidental. Vijay spoke alongside news that the National Payments Corporation of India launched three products at the same event — some of which could eventually go international — and the move follows other recent digital-diplomacy steps for the diaspora, including the Digital OCI Card and e-Arrival Card for Indian-origin foreign citizens. UIDAI also said it is preparing guidelines to let small merchants use Aadhaar-enabled authentication for KYC, alongside new "Aadhaar Lite" onboarding products.

The UAE pilot — and what's next

A parallel track is already running in the Gulf. India's International Financial Services Centres Authority is piloting Aadhaar face authentication in the UAE to onboard NRIs digitally, testing whether foreign IP addresses can access the Aadhaar application securely. The pilot is expected to extend to three more jurisdictions, including the US, with the system targeted to be in place by the end of the current financial year. For IFSCA, the push is part of a broader strategy to turn GIFT City into a hub through which the 36-million-strong diaspora — including high-net-worth individuals, family offices and globally dispersed Indian-origin businesses — can invest into India. HSBC and SBI have already set up wealth-management operations at GIFT City to serve that clientele.

What it means for NRIs and OCIs

If the framework lands, the practical payoff is large: remote KYC for Indian bank accounts and investments, easier property and tax documentation, and a single digital identity bridging the diaspora's financial life in two countries. The caveat is that this is still an official aspiration, not a notified rule. The legal framework, the interoperability design, and the security questions being stress-tested in the UAE pilot — all must resolve before a single NRI enrols from abroad.

What to watch

Watch for UIDAI's formal policy notification for OCI enrolment, the outcome of the UAE face-authentication pilot, and whether the US pilot gets announced — that will be the signal that global Aadhaar is moving from fireside-chat ambition to operational reality.
